entries.title: Russia opens first road bridge with North Korea
entries.summary: Russia and North Korea have opened their first road bridge across the Tumen River as political, economic and military ties between the two countries deepen.
entries.content:
Russian Federation

Russia opens first road bridge with North Korea

September 7, 2026

Russia and North Korea have opened their first road bridge across the Tumen River as political, economic and military ties between the two countries deepen.

Russia and North Korea on Monday cut the ribbon on the first road bridge linking the two countries as Moscow and Pyongyang deepen their strategic partnership.

The crossing spans the Tumen River and marks another expansion of transport links between the two countries.

Where is the new bridge?

The road crossing is near the existing Friendship Bridge, a railway bridge commissioned in 1959 following the Korean War.

Russia and North Korea already have direct rail and air connections, but until now there had been no road bridge between them.

The new bridge is named after Soviet Red Army officer Yakov Novichenko, who is credited with saving North Korean founder Kim Il Sung's life. Relatives of Novichenko attended the opening ceremony.

Construction began in April 2025 after the project was agreed during Russian President Vladimir Putin's visit to North Korea in 2024.

Why is the road bridge being opened now?

Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin said the new crossing should boost economic development, tourism and employment.

"I am convinced that the expansion of cross-border transport infrastructure will provide a powerful impetus for the further development of trade, economic, scientific, technological and cultural cooperation," the TASS news agency quoted Mishustin as saying by video link at the opening ceremony.

Relations between Moscow and Pyongyang have strengthened considerably since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

North Korea sent thousands of troops to Russia's Kursk region to help Russian forces repel a Ukrainian incursion launched in 2024.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: Can the AfD form a government in Saxony-Anhalt?
entries.summary: Following its record election success, the far-right Alternative for Germany aims to form a government. What options does it have without a majority?
entries.content:
Germany

Can the AfD form a government in Saxony-Anhalt?

September 7, 2026

Following its record election success, the far-right Alternative for Germany aims to form a government. What options does it have without a majority?

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) achieved its best-ever election result in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt, winning well over 40% of the vote and leaving all other parties far behind.

However, the party lacks the majority of seats in parliament needed to govern on its own. Because the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been classified as "confirmed far-right extremist" by the domestic intelligence agency, other parties announced that cooperation with the AfD was out of the question. This will make forming a government in this eastern German state quite difficult.

On election night, Ulrich Siegmund announced on public broadcaster ARD: "As a democrat, I will reach out to all those who wish to work with us to bring about a fundamental political turnaround." At the same time, he acknowledged that there are currently no political parties that he considers suitable for a coalition government.

Above all, he was referring to the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which currently holds power in coalitions both in Saxony-Anhalt and on the federal level in Germany. Siegmund, along with the entire AfD leadership, has characterized the CDU's policy of refusing to work with the AfD a failure.

On public broadcaster ZDF, AfD party co-leader Alice Weidel sharply criticized the CDU for stonewalling the AfD: "The CDU will not win another election — not a federal election. And this clearly gives the AfD a mandate to govern. Because we are democrats, we do not refuse to work with others."

On election night, Ulrich Siegmund emphasized that implementing the AfD's platform was more important to him than the prospect of power: "There will be no compromise with me." Leading up to the vote, the 35-year-old AfD lead candidate repeatedly stated that he was only interested in governing alone in order to usher in a fundamental political change in Germany.

The AfD's radical governing platform

For months, the AfD's political program has sparked heated debates across Germany. That's because the party wants to drastically tighten asylum and immigration policies. It wants to speed up the deportation of illegal asylum seekers and introduce a general work requirement for all other asylum seekers.

Above all, however, it wants to make Saxony-Anhalt and Germany less attractive to immigrants and is calling for a "180-degree turnaround in migration policy." During its election campaign, the party repeatedly blamed migrants for crime in German cities and for the housing shortage.

What's more, the AfD is planning a radical restructuring of society: it has declared war on public broadcasting, wants to cut funding for democracy projects, intends to establish a kind of vigilante group against migrants and aims to combat social diversity — all of which is laid out in its platform. And Ulrich Siegmund emphasized in an ARD interview that these issues are non-negotiable.

Now, one option involves a minority government led by the AfD, in which it would need to secure support from other parties to advance its policies.

AfD Chairwoman Alice Weidel told ZDF television: "Who ultimately forms the government — perhaps through a tolerance agreement or even a coalition — remains to be seen."

On behalf of the CDU, the party's secretary-general, Franziska Hoppermann, categorically ruled out a coalition: "There will be no cooperation with the far left or the far right."

Could the BSW help the AfD form a government?

The biggest unknown in this power struggle is the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), should it manage to move into the state parliament.

The small party campaigns primarily on a left-wing economic platform and — similar to the AfD — calls for a foreign policy that is more friendly toward Russia. In the past, party founder and former member of the socialist Left Party, Sahra Wagenknecht, has repeatedly expressed openness to substantive cooperation with the AfD. However, for ideological reasons, the party is not considered a particularly attractive partner within AfD circles.

As the AfD celebrated its victory into the night and even before the vote count was complete, some AfD state politicians announced that, if necessary, they intended to remain in the opposition and keep the other parties on the defensive until they could secure a majority of their own.

Take, for example, Oliver Kirchner, co-chair of the AfD caucus in the state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt: "If we end up behind the lectern as the opposition, it will be brutal for the others," he warned during an AfD livestream.

This article has been translated from German.

entries.title: Middle East: Israeli strikes kill several in Lebanon
entries.summary: Lebanon's Health Ministry said at least 10 were killed in overnight Israeli strikes in the south of the country. Meanwhile, traffic in the Strait of Hormuz has sunk to its lowest level since May. DW has more.
entries.content:
Middle East

Middle East: Israeli strikes kill several in Lebanon

Published September 7, 2026last updated September 7, 2026

Lebanon's Health Ministry said at least 10 were killed in overnight Israeli strikes in the south of the country. Meanwhile, traffic in the Strait of Hormuz has sunk to its lowest level since May. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

Below is a roundup of headlines from the wider Middle East region on Monday, September 7.

  • Lebanon's Health Ministry said 10 were killed, including 2 children, after Israeli strikes
  • Maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz has reached its lowest level since May
  • Israel says it has struck Hamas infrastructure in Gaza

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Oman evacuates 16 crew from attacked oil tanker

Oman evacuates 16 crew from attacked oil tanker

Sixteen crew members on board Saudi-flagged oil tanker, attacked by Iran, have been evacuated, according to Oman's Maritime Security Centre.

"A Royal Navy of Oman (RNO) vessel provided logistical support to the tanker's 25-member crew and evacuated 16 crew members," the Oman MSC said.

Last Wednesday, Saudi ​Arabia said the attack on ⁠the tanker, ​owned by ​national shipping company Bahri, had ​killed two Filipino ‌seafarers.

The status of the seven not accounted ⁠for ​yet is not immediately known.

Skip next section Germany urges UN's top court to quash Israel genocide case

Germany urges UN's top court to quash Israel genocide case

Germany's top legal representative has told the UN's top court that a genocide case over weapons sales to Israel, should be thrown out.

The matter was brought by Nicaragua and Germany's top lawyer, Julia Monar, said the judges at the International Court of Justice lacked the jurisdiction to rule on the case , dismissing Nicaragua's allegations of Berlin "facilitating genocide" as "inaccurate and distorted."

Nicaragua argues that Germany's backing of Israel, notably in terms of arms exports, contravenes the 1948 UN Genocide Convention.

"Nicaragua’s conduct indicates that it was not interested in hearing Germany’s view on its allegations, but simply in bringing Germany before this court," Monar, told the judges.

Monar said that Nicaragua failed to properly notify the German government and gave her country less than a month to reply before launching proceedings.

It's typically expected that countries attempt to resolve disputes before bringing them to the court.

Monar pointed out that Berlin scrutinizes all exports of military equipment in accordance with international law.

"Germany has not, since 2024, authorized an export of weapons of war, with final destination in Israel that can be used in the Gaza conflict,” she said.

The German government operates what it calls a "case by case" approval process of arms sales to Israel, with the stated goal of avoiding anything that might be used in Gaza, where at least 73,000 Palestinians were killed between the October 7, 2023 Hamas attacks on Israeli civlians and late August of this year.

However, Germany only instituted this policy in 2025, and continued to ship defensive equipment worth hundreds of millions of euros this year.

Skip next section Iran issues warning as South Korea mulls Hormuz contribution

Iran issues warning as South Korea mulls Hormuz contribution

Iran's Foreign Ministry issued a warning against any country participating in security operations in the Strait of Hormuz.

"Any military deployment or participation in operations by other countries in the Persian Gulf or the Strait of Hormuz can only be regarded as direct support for the party responsible for that aggression and will have serious consequences," Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said in a post on X.

Baqaei noted Tehran's diplomatic relationship with Seoul, saying that Iran "places great importance on its friendly relations with the Republic of Korea."

The comments come after South Korea's presidency on Friday said it had not reached a decision on sending forces to the Strait of Hormuz to help ensure free navigation of the waterway.

South Korea has been facing pressure from the Trump administration to make military contributions relating to Iran and has been accused of turning down any request for assistance.

"We are closely communicating with the international community, including relevant countries, to help restore peace and stability in the Middle East as soon as possible and to ensure the free passage of all vessels, including those of our country, through the Strait of Hormuz," Yonhap news agency cited South Korea's Foreign Ministry as saying in a statement.

Skip next section Shipping traffic in Strait of Hormuz drops following US-Iran strikes

Shipping traffic in Strait of Hormuz drops following US-Iran strikes

Maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz has dropped to the lowest level since May , according to data analytics platform Kpler.

According to its latest figures, an average of 10 commodity vessels, transited the vital shipping route over the past 10 days.

Kpler recorded the number on Sunday, which was down from the 15 vessels on Friday and the 13 seen on Saturday.

The drop in maritime traffic comes amid strikes targeting tankers by the US and Iran.

On Saturday, US forces hit three Iranian oil tankers, following Iranian attacks on US warships in the region.

In retaliation, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it has targeted three oil tankers travelling what it said ewas an unathorized route in the strait.

The strikes over the weekend represented a "major escalation in maritime conflict," the Reuters news agency cited maritime intelligence firm Marisks as saying.

"Commercial tankers are now being deliberately used as instruments of reciprocal economic pressure, substantially weakening the previous distinction between military confrontation and commercial shipping," Marisks noted.

"Risk is therefore assessed as extreme for Iranian/Iran-linked tonnage ​and materially elevated for US-linked or US-escorted shipping throughout the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman," the firm said

 

Skip next section WATCH: How much oil is getting through the Strait of Hormuz?

WATCH: How much oil is getting through the Strait of Hormuz?

Despite months of conflict, attacks on Gulf states and continuing disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, oil supplies remain well above worst-case forecasts. Why? Energy expert Ben Cahill shares his insights with DW.

Skip next section Reports of at least 10 dead following overnight Israeli strikes

Reports of at least 10 dead following overnight Israeli strikes

Overnight Israeli strikes in southern Lebanon killed at least 10 people, including two children, health officials said.

Earlier, Lebanon's National News Agency (NNA) reported that Israeli warplanes struck a residential building in Kfar Rumman in southern Lebanon.

The agency reported that a separate drone strike struck a vehicle with two medics inside, however, the Associated Press cited the Health Ministry as saying the strike on the car killed one paramedic and wounded two others.

Israel's military has not commented on these latest strikes, but Israel's Foreign Ministry released a statement on X referencing the militant group.

"Repeated drone attacks. Weapons storage. Terror infrastructure. Command centres embedded in civilian areas. Hezbollah continues attempting to rebuild its military capabilities in southern Lebanon. These violations will not be accepted," Israel's Foreign Ministry wrote on X.

The ministry said that Hezbollah had violated the Israel-Lebanon ceasefire agreement, under which, the militant group would be disarmed.

"Hezbollah continues attempting to rebuild its military capabilities in southern Lebanon," the ministry said.

On Sunday, Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun pushed for Washington and the international community to help stop Israeli attacks.

Despite a peace agreement that came into effect over two months ago, flare-ups are continuing between Israel and Hezbollah.

The US, Germany and several Arab countries consider Hezbollah a terrorist organization, whereas the EU only deems Hezbollah's armed wing a terror group.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

We're following developments from southern Lebanon following reports that Israeli strikes have killed at least 10 people, including two children.

It comes after the a warning notice from Israel's military that it was targeting a "Hezbollah terrorist facility."

Meanwhile, according to the latest shipping data, traffic in the Strait of Hormuz has dipped to the lowest level since May following US and Iranian strikes on tankers.

entries.title: Ukraine: Zelenskyy says war looks set to go on into winter
entries.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says there appears to be no end in sight in Russia's war against his country. His words come after another round of US-led diplomacy. DW has the latest.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine: Zelenskyy says war looks set to go on into winter

Published September 7, 2026last updated September 7, 2026

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says there appears to be no end in sight in Russia's war against his country. His words come after another round of US-led diplomacy. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Ukraine's president says the war with Russia appears likely to continue into winter
  • His comments came after talks with visiting US envoys produced no announced breakthrough
  • Russian officials say Ukrainian drone attacks killed two people in separate strikes in the Perm and Belgorod regions

Here are the latest developments in Russia's war in Ukraine on Monday, September 7:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Russia, North Korea open first road bridge

Russia, North Korea open first road bridge

Russia and North Korea have opened their first road bridge across the Tumen River, expanding transport links as political, economic and military ties between Moscow and Pyongyang deepen.

Read more about the story here.

Skip next section Ukrainian drone attacks kill 2 in Russia, officials say

Ukrainian drone attacks kill 2 in Russia, officials say

Attacks with drones killed at least two people and injured several others in Russia, regional authorities have said.

One person was killed and four others were injured in Russia's Perm region after a drone attack damaged a residential building, regional Governor Dmitry Makhonin said.

He said local air defense units had shot down 27 Ukranian drones over the region, which lies deep inside Russia.

In the Belgorod region, which borders Ukraine, one person was killed and another injured in a separate Ukrainian drone attack, according to local authorities.

Reuters said it could not independently verify the reports. There was no immediate comment from Ukraine.

Skip next section No end in sight after diplomatic effort, says Zelenskyy

No end in sight after diplomatic effort, says Zelenskyy

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the war with Russia currently appears likely to continue into the winter, after talks with visiting US envoys in Kyiv.

The talks produced upbeat assessments from both sides but no announced breakthrough in efforts to end the war.

"We very much hope that we will be able to reach agreements with our American partners, and we are counting on the support of our European partners if the war continues in winter — and this is how it appears at the moment," Zelenskyy said.

He also said Ukraine would hold talks with the US, France and Germany, without giving further details.

Zelenskyy again argued that the most difficult territorial issues could only be resolved in a meeting between leaders.

US envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, had traveled to Kyiv a day after meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.

Putin had announced a three-day pause in attacks on Kyiv for the duration of the US negotiators' visit. Ukraine, in turn, refrained from attacking Moscow during the same period.

Zelenskyy joked that the presence of Witkoff and Kushner had "worked better than the Patriot air defense systems."

It was Witkoff and Kushner’s first visit to the Ukrainian capital, a repeated target of Russian strikes since the start of Moscow's full-scale invasion. The pair have made several visits to Moscow.

While Witkoff and Zelenskyy both described Sunday's talks positively, neither side announced a concrete breakthrough.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

You join us after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy downplayed hopes of a quick end to the conflict, saying the fighting currently appears likely to continue into winter.

He was speaking after talks in Kyiv with US envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law.

Meanwhile, Russian officials say Ukrainian drone attacks have killed at least two people and injured several others.

entries.title: UK government condemns 'thuggish' anti-migrant protests in Portsmouth
entries.summary: Hundreds gathered in Portsmouth after some refugees arrived by boat from France, a day after masked protesters disrupted traffic at the port of Dover.
entries.content:
September 7, 2026

Hundreds gathered in Portsmouth after some refugees arrived by boat from France, a day after masked protesters disrupted traffic at the port of Dover.

British minister Emma Reynolds on Monday slammed "thuggish" anti-migrant protests that blocked roads in the English coastal city of Portsmouth.

Hundreds of protesters gathered in Portsmouth on Sunday following the arrival of about 140 migrants who had crossed the English Channel from France, UK media reported.

"This is thuggish and intimidating behavior," Reynolds, who is Chief Secretary to the Treasury, told Sky News, adding that the police brought the Portsmouth protest under control.

The demonstration came a day after masked protesters disrupted traffic at Dover terminal, blocking routes to the busy ferry port.

Masked protesters in Dover

On Saturday, hundreds of masked people blocked traffic at England's port of Dover as part of an anti-migrant protest, halting ferry traffic between France and the UK.

Video footage showed demonstrators, reportedly backed by far-right groups, in balaclavas chanting "stop the boats," in a reference to refugees and migrants who attempt the dangerous English Channel crossing in a bid to reach Great Britain.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham's Labour Party government said that "the right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but we condemn the behavior in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused."

The Dover demonstration caused a traffic jam of about four miles (6.4 km) and temporarily halted traffic into and out of the port.

Britain has struggled for years to curb small-boat crossings from France, although Reynolds said arrivals were down 43% from last year to about 17,000 so far this year.

entries.title: India news: Rescue efforts underway in deadly Delhi building collapse
entries.summary: The building was located in New Delhi's Satya Niketan, popular among students from nearby colleges and universities. At least 12 people have been rescued from the rubble. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India news: Several dead in Delhi building collapse

Published September 7, 2026last updated September 7, 2026

The building was located in New Delhi's Satya Niketan, popular among students from nearby colleges and universities. At least 12 people have been rescued from the rubble. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • At least seven people have died after a building collapsed in Delhi

  • The building was located in South Delhi's Satya Niketan, popular among Delhi University students

  • Rescue operations are underway

Below is a roundup of the top headlines from India on Monday, September 7.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section India's food warning labels challenged in court

India's food warning labels challenged in court

Indian health activists have filed the first formal court objection to the government's proposed food warning labels, calling the plan an "industry-friendly loophole" that lets many unhealthy products avoid scrutiny.

The Indian government has proposed that a red hexagonal label be added if a food exceeds limits in at least two of three concerning nutrients: added sugar, salt or saturated fat.

Nonprofit group 3S And Our Health told the Supreme Court the proposal would let high-risk items slip through, as a product high in just one nutrient would not be flagged, the filing, as accessed by Reuters new agency, said.

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has also drawn criticism over exemptions for foods like honey and jaggery.

Health activists have been pushing for front-of-pack warning labels for years, but it remains unclear how effective they will be in their current form.

"After years of advocacy, and after the Supreme Court pushed the issue, FSSAI has accepted a front-of-pack warning. That fight is won. The next fight is not whether there will be a label, but whether the label will tell the truth," Dr Arun Gupta, paediatrician and Convenor, Nutrition Advocacy in Public Interest (NAPi) told Firstpost.

The Indian government intends to make rules stricter by having warning labels for each concerning nutrient in the second phase of the plan, a source told The Telegraph newspaper.

According to a study published in The Lancet journal, India had 180 million adults who were overweight or obese in 2021. The number is projected to rise to 450 million by 2050.

The case will be heard on September 10.

Skip next section Drone scare at Amritsar airport prompts flight diversions: reports

Drone scare at Amritsar airport prompts flight diversions: reports

Multiple suspected drones were spotted around the operational area of Amritsar's international airport Sunday night, Indian news agency ANI reported, prompting authorities to divert seven flights.

Airport Director Anirudh Kumar said the Air Traffic Control (ATC) unit received information from the Indian Air Force at around 9.45 pm local time regarding suspected drone activity over the airfield. This prompted all flight operations to be suspended for 90 minutes.

"Two of the flights were diverted to Chandigarh and five of them were diverted to Delhi," a Delhi airport official told the Hindustan Times.

Malaysia Airlines, Air India, Air India Express and IndiGo flights were among those diverted, local news agencies reported.

Amritsar's Sri Guru Ram Dass Jee International Airport is located about 30 kilometers (~18 miles) from India's border with Pakistan.

Reports suggested that the drones may have been flown locally, but the sensitive nature of the airport’s location prompted swift security action from all agencies involved.

Amritsar police told the Indian Express that the drones were flown during a sports tournament in a nearby village.

"These drones originated from the video recording of a sports tournament. Drones were used for this purpose without permission. It is not allowed to fly drones in 8 kilometres radius of the airport. We will take legal action in this matter," said Raja Sansi Station House Officer Gurpreet Singh.

Skip next section At least 7 people killed as rescue efforts continue

At least 7 people killed as rescue efforts continue

The death toll has risen to seven after rescue personnel recovered another body amid the rubble of a five-story building in India's capital city Monday, a day after the nearly 50-year-old structure came crashing down. 

The building was located in Satya Niketan, a popular student hub that houses hundreds of university students often living in crowded conditions. It is situated in close proximity to Delhi University's South Campus, making it a popular destination for students.

Local media reported that the building housed a private hostel.

In its latest update, Delhi Police said a total of 12 people had been rescued during the operation. Emergency crews say more people may be trapped in the rubble.

Rescue teams, including personnel from disaster agencies as well as fire and police teams, were using heavy machinery and sniffer dogs to locate those trapped.

Earlier, the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), which is treating victims of the collapse, said its trauma center received 10 people: "Out of the 10 patients, five were brought dead, while one patient who was in critical condition later succumbed to his injuries."

Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta addressed the potential cause of the collapse, saying: "It is certain that there was ‌water in the building's basement, and due ‌to ​accumulation of water, due to ongoing repair work, the old building collapsed."

The police have registered a First Information Report (FIR) under Sections 105, 290 and 125(a) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (the official criminal code of India) against the building owners, local media reported. The specific sections relate to culpable homicide, negligence in the construction or repair of buildings as well as acts that endanger human life.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello! This is Seerat from DW's Studio Delhi, bringing you the latest from across India.

We are back, reporting on the building collapse in an area frequented by Delhi University students, including me (albeit over 10 years ago).

Rescue operations are underway, putting the lack of infrastructure, which forces students to opt for private housing options amid a severe lack of college hostels, into the spotlight.

For this and more, follow our live blog.

entries.title: Jamaica to petition King Charles over slavery reparations
entries.summary: Jamaica will ask King Charles III to refer questions about the legality of slavery and Britain's potential obligation to provide reparations.
entries.content:
September 7, 2026

Jamaica will ask King Charles III to refer questions about the legality of slavery and Britain's potential obligation to provide reparations.

The Jamaican government will petition King Charles III on Monday as the country seeks "reparations for the African ancestors who suffered under hundreds of years of enslavement," the Culture Ministry said.

Culture Minister Olivia Grange is leading a delegation which will ask the king, Jamaica's head of state, to refer three questions to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, the island's highest court of appeal in London.

The three questions on the legality of the trans-Atlantic slave trade are:

  • Whether the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica was legal under English law
  • Whether it broke international law, and
  • Whether Britain now has a legal duty to provide redress

Jamaica says the petition would be the first time a Commonwealth country has used the legal route to pursue reparatory justice.

What did Jamaica say about reparation for slavery?

Grange pointed to Britain's £20 million (€23.28 million) compensation payment to slave owners following the abolition of slavery in 1833.

"Up to 2015, Britain was paying the slave masters, because we were being considered property," Grange said.

"The question really should be: if in modern times we're still paying back the slave masters for the property that was our people, our ancestors, for property that was because of the abolition of slavery, then why shouldn't we be pursuing some remedy at this time?"

Grange said Jamaica wanted the legal questions answered before deciding on its next steps.

The Jamaican delegation will also meet British Museum officials to discuss the return of colonial-era artefacts.

A Buckingham Palace spokesperson said the king has expressed his "commitment to promoting greater understanding around the issue of slavery and finding ways to address historic wrongs."

While Caribbean nations, in recent years have called for an apology and measures including debt relief, the British government has said it will not pay slavery reparations.

Trans-Atlantic slave trade then and now

The trans-Atlantic slave trade between the 15th and 19th centuries involved Europeans (and later Americans) facilitating kidnappings, then transporting and enslaving of millions of Africans to their colonies in the Americas and the Caribbean.

An estimated 12–15 million Africans were forcibly transported across the Atlantic over four centuries, with about 10.7 million surviving the journey to the Americas. Up to 2 million died during the crossing.

Haiti gained independence from France in 1804 after a successful slave revolt, but France forced the new state in 1825 to pay 150 million gold francs to former slaveholders as compensation for "lost property," threatening war if it refused.

It took Haiti more than a hundred years to settle the debt plunging the Caribbean into a long-term cycle of poverty.

The legacy of slavery remains a contentious issue. Earlier in March, when the United Nations General Assembly voted to recognize the enslavement of Africans during the trans-Atlantic slave trade as "the gravest crime against humanity," the United Kingdom and European Union member states abstained, while the United States, Israel and Argentina voted against the resolution.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: Saxony-Anhalt: Germany wakes up to 'unsettling' AfD victory
entries.summary: The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won the Saxony-Anhalt state election but without an absolute majority in parliament. Other European nations were wrestling with the impact of the results. Follow DW.
entries.content:
Jon Shelton|

Akanksha Saxena|

Richard Connor| Patrick Große |

Felix Tamsut|

Zac Crellin|

Darko Janjevic|

Louis Oelofsewith dpa, AFP, AP, KNA, Reuters

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won the Saxony-Anhalt state election but without an absolute majority in parliament. Other European nations were wrestling with the impact of the results. Follow DW.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Far-right AfD hails 'sensational' results in the Saxony-Anhalt vote
  • AfD expected to struggle with coalition building as many parties reject cooperation
  • Left-wing populist BSW open to working with AfD on some issues
  • Merz's CDU suffers worst Saxony-Anhalt result since German reunification
  • The European press calling the results an "unsettling new page in German history"

Germany's Saxony-Anhalt state held an election on Sunday, September 6. Follow all the developments on Monday, September 7, here.

Skip next section Neighboring France voices concern over rise of the AfD

Neighboring France voices concern over rise of the AfD

Speaking with RTL Radio on Monday morning, French Finance Minister Roland Lescure said the far-right AfD's resounding victory in German state elections, "sends a very, very worrying signal."

Lescure called the victory part of a "populist wave" that is "spreading around the world today," saying "we must resist" it.

Lescure's comments echoed those delivered by France's Minister of European Affairs Benjamin Haddad, who called the victory "a very grave moment for Europe."

For years, France has faced the prospect of a far-right government as Marine Le Pen's ultraconservative National Rally (RN) party has come ever closer to gaining power in successive elections, a situation that will repeat itself during federal elections there next year.

It should be noted that RN ended cooperation with the AfD in the European Parliament for its revisionist view of Nazi Germany, it's ties with far-right extremists and allegations that it aided Chinese and Russian agents in Brussels.

Skip next section AfD leaders say migrants 'have nothing to fear as long as they contribute to making Germany a better place'

AfD leaders say migrants 'have nothing to fear as long as they contribute to making Germany a better place'

Candidate Ulrich Siegmund said he would seek to become the state's premier during a Q&A session after Monday morning's press conference but noted that he would need a stable majority if he was to have a chance to turn the state around.

He also said those with immigration backgrounds need not fear the AfD, claiming that even anti-fascists had been convinced about his earnestness during discussions in which he engaged with protesters outside campaign rallies.

Party co-leader Alice Weidel said the AfD is not anti-immigrant per se and that it welcomes all foreigners willing to "contribute to making Germany a better place" before railing against unqualified immigrants receiving German taxpayer funds as welfare.

Neither Siegmund nor Weidel provided evidence or data to back up their claims.

She also emphasized what she called the fears of women, children and others in the face of "criminal immigrants" and called for far tighter borders, pointing out that Germany's major parties had lost touch with reality in opening them.

This came despite the fact that crime statistics show that immigrants make up only a small minority of criminal suspects, with age and gender being a much more decisive factor.

Moments after saying the party was not against immigrants, Weidel then doubled down on the party's promise to deport as many immigrants as possible as soon as it took power, saying Germany could not afford what she called an "open-border policy."

Germany has increased border controls and security in recent months and net migration and asylum applications have already dropped significantly over the past two years.

Skip next section AfD calls for political cooperation, ultimately federal leadership at press conference

AfD calls for political cooperation, ultimately federal leadership at press conference

In their first press conference since yesterday's Saxony-Anhalt state elections, Alternative for Germany (AfD) co-leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla, alongside top state candidate Ulrich Siegmund, called the Sunday result "historic" and suggested other parties reconsider the "failed concept" of the so-called "firewall" to honor voters' wishes and help the AfD run the state. 

Weidel started off by thanking voters who came out to show support for the party despite "negative press coverage" — the charge of "fake news" and "unfair media coverage" was a through-line for all three party representatives during the press conference.

Weidel praised historically high voter turnout before slamming existing political parties, specifically Chancellor Friedrich Merz, for whom she has a particular animosity, and running through a laundry list of issues that motivated AfD voters — immigration, immigrant crime, high prices, energy policy and de-industrialization being foremost among them.

Weidel then went on to declare that the country's two largest popular parties, the CDU and SPD, would "never win another election" because they had failed to find solutions to those problems.

Co-leader Tino Chrupalla praised candidate Ulrich Siegmund before also slamming Merz — whom he called "arrogant" for dismissing the AfD as a laboratory for political malcontents — while looking forward to coming elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and criticizing German support for Ukraine in its war against Russia.

After claiming the so-called political "firewall" had collapsed, Chrupalla said the AfD is prepared to hold talks with other political parties, including the CDU, which he said would "disappear" if it did not change course.

After thanking AfD leadership, candidate Siegmund joined in slamming the CDU, Chancellor Merz and the media. Siegmund claimed that tens of thousands of supporters had turned out for AfD rallies during the election campaign — though such numbers have been seen as being exaggerated.

Siegmund said Sunday's result had shown that hope had triumphed over "fake news" to deliver a clear mandate for the AfD to form a government.

Further, Siegmund railed against broken political promises — focusing specifically on Merz and the CDU — vowing that he and the AfD would "stay true to our values" and claiming, "people are finally trusting politicians again."

Lastly, Siegmund claimed the vote was, "not only important for the state of Saxony-Anhalt but the entire nation," saying he needed a "Chancellor Alice Weidel" to help him turn the country around, before promising to slash foreign aid to help Germany and its citizens.

"This is not just about Saxony-Anhalt, it's about Germany," he said. "We want our old, safe Germany back again."

Skip next section What are the coalition possibilites in Saxony-Anhalt?

What are the coalition possibilites in Saxony-Anhalt?

Skip next section Holocaust survivor: 'This election result scares me'

Holocaust survivor: 'This election result scares me'

Holocaust survivor Eva Umlauf, president of the Berlin-based International Auschwitz Committee, on Monday told Germany's Catholic News Agency (KNA), "this election result scares me."

Umlauf then asked, "What path is Germany on? The one that it traveled before?"

After saying Holocaust survivors "never thought it possible" that a right-wing extremist party would again be voted into power at the state level — the AfD was also the largest faction voted into Thuringia's state parliament in 2024 — she added that she would continue to fight for democracy and for the memory of those six million Jews killed during the Nazi era. 

Umlauf said survivors "owe it to our murdered relatives" to keep their memory alive, calling it "our obligation to young people in Germany."

Skip next section Far-right AfD on the rise (mostly) for 10 years now

Far-right AfD on the rise (mostly) for 10 years now

Germany's far-right AfD has seen an almost constant rise in popularity since it was founded as an anti-euro party in April 2013.

After capitalizing on concerns about then-Chancellor Angela Merkel's immigration policies, the party saw a slight drop in popularity in 2019 amid infighting and backlash against right-wing political violence before latching onto its next theme — what it described as "government overreach" during the Coronavirus pandemic.

Skip next section Preliminary official results confirm AfD short of ruling majority despite landslide victory

Preliminary official results confirm AfD short of ruling majority despite landslide victory

The preliminary official results from Sunday's state elections have confirmed the AfD's historic win with tabulations remaining unchanged from a few hours prior.

The far-right party captured 39 seats in all, meaning it eclipsed all other competitors, yet fell just shy of winning an outright ruling majority.

Skip next section International press calls AfD win a 'clear signal'

International press calls AfD win a 'clear signal'

Outside Germany, international observers have called Sunday's AfD electoral victory in Saxony-Anhalt a "clear signal" for establishment parties.

New York's Wall Street Journal pointed to liberal immigration policy and weak economic performance as major contributors to the win, writing that conservative Chancellor Friedrich Merz had disappointed voters despite exhibiting the right economic and foreign policy reform instincts. The WSJ called the victory a "warning" that voters could ultimately gamble on letting the AfD lead the country alone.

In Italy, La Repubblica described an "unsettling new page in German history," noting that Saxony-Anhalt's voters — who represent only three percent of Germany's overall population — had betrayed the vow "never again" by choosing a rightwing extremist party espousing the "inhumane ideas" of the Nazi era to run their state.

Milan's Corriere della Sera echoed that sentiment, saying that Germany would "never be the same," and emphasizing that the whole of Europe seems as if "hypnotized by the extreme right."

And in Spain, El Pais wrote that the vote would force Europe's democrats to rethink the tired approach of either imitating far-right extremists in hopes of siphoning off voters or attempting to isolate them. The paper pointed to the AfD in Germany but also France's National Rally (RN) as examples of establishment parties failing to hold back extremists despite the clear moral and political imperative of rejecting cooperation with parties that "question the founding principles of post war democracies."

Skip next section Elon Musk congratulates AfD on election victory in Saxony-Anhalt

Elon Musk congratulates AfD on election victory in Saxony-Anhalt

Tech entrepreneur and the world's richest man, Elon Musk, who has backed Germany’s far-right AfD, congratulated the party on its Saxony-Anhalt election victory. 

"Gut gemacht!" (Well Done!) Musk wrote on his social media platform X in response to a post by AfD co-leader Alice Weidel congratulating the party's lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund on the result in Saxony-Anhalt.



Siegmund promptly replied to Musk, thanking him for his "support."

"If we take responsibility here, I would very much welcome the opportunity for strong and constructive cooperation. Germany would once again be a place worth investing in," Siegmund wrote.

Since Donald Trump returned to the White House, the AfD has strengthened its ties with Washington, with Alice Weidel calling the US president a role model and AfD representatives attending his inauguration.

Elon Musk, then a close Trump adviser, openly campaigned for the AfD and continues to back far-right political figures.

Skip next section Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance sees a 'political reset'

Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance sees a 'political reset'

Sahra Wagenknecht, founder of the populist BSW, called for a "political reset" in Saxony-Anhalt after the party narrowly cleared the 5% threshold to enter the state parliament.

"There are hopefully now majorities in the Magdeburg state parliament for a change in energy policy, an end to the Russia sanctions, better education and a fundamental reform of public broadcasting," Wagenknecht told dpa.

Since its founding in January 2024, Wagenknecht’s BSW has positioned itself as economically left-wing but culturally conservative. She supports higher minimum wages and rent caps but also backs tougher immigration policies.

She has repeatedly blamed the West for Russia’s war in Ukraine and opposed sanctions against Moscow. BSW politicians, like some AfD figures, have also been accused of maintaining ties with supporters of Russian President Vladimir Putin.

"The BSW’s comeback has begun," she said, adding "the result would boost her party’s campaign ahead of state elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin."

The far-right AfD fell short of an outright majority, leaving the shape of a government in Saxony-Anhalt unclear. Wagenknecht has ruled out a coalition with the AfD but not cooperation, potentially giving her party the balance of power.

"The policy of keeping the AfD out of government has failed. Simply trying to form another coalition to exclude the AfD would be an affront to voters." she said.

Skip next section AfD faces uncertain coalition options after Saxony-Anhalt win

AfD faces uncertain coalition options after Saxony-Anhalt win

According to preliminary official results, the AfD emerged as the largest party but fell short of a governing majority in the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament. The far-right party therefore faces challenges in forming a government.

AfD lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt Ulrich Siegmund said his party’s result represented "a clear mandate to govern."

At the same time, the 35-year-old said he currently saw no potential coalition partners. However, he added that he did not know what might happen in the coming days.

"I don’t know whether there are individual lawmakers who might say: 'That’s it, I’m not playing along with this anymore,'" he said, adding, "A lot can still happen." Following the historic win, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla said: "Ulrich Siegmund will definitely run as a candidate for state premier in the state parliament. That much is certain."

If efforts to form a government fail, Siegmund said a new election could also be an option. "In the worst-case scenario, there would simply be new elections, and then we would get 50% or 55%," he said.

Is coalition without AfD possible?

The only coalition that would have a numerical majority without the AfD would be an alliance of all the other parties. However, under a resolution adopted previously, the center-right CDU rules out not only a coalition with the AfD but also with the Left Party. This policy is known as the " political firewall."

That would also be a stumbling block for a CDU-led minority government. In addition, the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) could potentialy hold the balance of power with five seats. Its leadership has ruled out supporting CDU.

Following the election, the previously governing coalition of the CDU, SPD and FDP will end. However, state premier Sven Schulze and his Cabinet will remain in office in a caretaker capacity until a new state premier is elected.

Skip next section Is Germany’s "political firewall" against the AfD collapsing?

Is Germany’s "political firewall" against the AfD collapsing?

Germany’s mainstream parties have long maintained a "political firewall" against cooperation with the far-right Alternative for Germany. But that firewall is under growing pressure following the AfD’s historic win in the Saxony-Anhalt state election and prospects in other forthcoming state elections.

The term refers to efforts by established parties to prevent extremist parties from gaining political influence through cooperation or shared votes. The center-right CDU formally rejected cooperation with the AfD in 2018.

But in January 2025, a CDU motion in the Bundestag passed with AfD support, prompting accusations that Chancellor Friedrich Merz had breached the firewall.

The AfD’s growing electoral strength is now raising fresh questions about how long the firewall can hold and what its future means for Germany’s political center.

Read here for more context: What is the 'political firewall' against Germany's far-right AfD?

Skip next section AfD wins most votes in Saxony-Anhalt, preliminary official results show

AfD wins most votes in Saxony-Anhalt, preliminary official results show

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won 43.8% of the vote in Germany's Saxony-Anhalt state election, according to preliminary official results, making it the largest party, but falling short of a governing majority in the regional parliament.

Six parties will be represented in the state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt, which has 83 seats:

  • Alternative for Germany (AfD) — 43.8%, 39 seats
  • Christian Democratic Union (CDU) — 17.2%, 15 seats
  • Social Democratic Party (SPD) — 9.3%, 8 seats
  • Green Party — 8.9%, 8 seats
  • Left Party — 8.6%, 8 seats
  • Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) — 5.3%, 5 seats

Meanwhile, the business-focused Free Democrats (FDP) secured only 2.6% of the vote, failing to reach the 5% threshold.

According to the preliminary results, turnout was almost 78%, the highest in Saxony-Anhalt since German reunification in 1990.

Skip next section WATCH: "Migration alone no longer explains the party’s rise"

WATCH: "Migration alone no longer explains the party’s rise"

Historian Katja Hoyer says the AfD's breakthrough was fueled by a more upbeat campaign around Ulrich Siegmund, while mainstream parties struggled to offer a positive vision of change.

Skip next section CDU fails to win a single direct mandate in Saxony-Anhalt state election

CDU fails to win a single direct mandate in Saxony-Anhalt state election

As a major setback for Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s center-right CDU, the party came away empty-handed in the individual constituencies.

The CDU failed to win a single direct mandate in the Saxony-Anhalt state election.

According to preliminary figures from the state election authority, CDU candidates were defeated in all 41 constituencies.

Alternative for Germany (AfD) candidates prevailed in 38 constituencies, including lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund in Genthin. Candidates from the Left Party won the remaining three constituencies: one in Magdeburg and two in Halle.

In the 2021 state election, the CDU won direct mandates in 40 of the 41 constituencies, while the AfD won one.

In Germany, voters have two votes. The "first vote" determines the winner of a constituency and the direct mandate. The "second vote" determines the distribution of seats among parties in the state parliament.

entries.title: Von der Leyen in Greenland with EU investments amid Trump pressure
entries.summary: The EU is preparing a major investment package and closer political ties with the Danish Arctic territory amid Donald Trump's demand for greater US control of the mineral-rich island.
entries.content:
Denmark

Von der Leyen visits Greenland amid Trump pressure

September 7, 2026

The EU is preparing a major investment package and closer political ties with the Danish Arctic territory amid Donald Trump's demand for greater US control of the mineral-rich island.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is in Greenland for a two-day visit as the European Union plans a major boost in investment in the region amid threats of US annexation under President Donald Trump.

Alongside the EU investments, she is expected to announce closer political ties with the autonomous Arctic territory which is part of the Kingdom of Denmark.

The European Commission head arrived in Greenland's capital Nuuk on Sunday in a show of support for Greenland and Denmark, and was received by Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.

In a post on X, Von der Leyen said the EU is committed to "contributing to a safe, peaceful Arctic and to the security of Greenland."

What does the EU investment package include?

The EU package is expected to include hundreds of millions of euros in investment in:

  • critical minerals,
  • satellite communications
  • renewable energy

Von der Leyen said the package would be "substantial" but gave no details.

Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen described the visit as an opportunity to deepen the territory's "close friendship and good partnership" with the EU.

The largely autonomous Greenland left the EU in 1985, although its population of about 57,000 are EU citizens through Danish citizenship.

Why is Trump demanding 'total access' over Greenland?

Von der Leyen's visit comes as the Arctic gains strategic importance for the US, Russia, China and Europe, with melting sea ice opening new shipping routes and increasing access to the region's mineral resources.

Trump has repeatedly stated that the US "needs" Greenland for its "national security," pointing to his claims — without providing evidence — that the island is "covered with Chinese and Russian ships all over the place."

Trump has maintained that Denmark cannot adequately defend the island against China and Russia.

His campaign bid to gain "total access" to the Danish territory has strained US-European relations and raised tensions within NATO as both Greenland and the Danish government have rejected Trump's demands.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: Several killed in Amazon cargo plane crash in Miami
entries.summary: At least five people have died after a cargo plane crashed at Miami International Airport. The aircraft overran a runway, struck several vehicles and caught fire.
entries.content:
United States of America

Several killed in Amazon cargo plane crash in Miami

September 7, 2026

At least five people have died after a cargo plane crashed at Miami International Airport. The aircraft overran a runway, struck several vehicles and caught fire.

An Amazon cargo plane barreled off a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday, killing at least five people as it struck vehicles and burst into flames, authorities said.

The aircraft overran the runway around 2 p.m. local time, or 18:00 GMT, after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico. Five people were killed, three critically injured and two others hospitalized with less severe injuries, Miami-Dade County officials said at a press conference.

"Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being and care of everyone involved. We’re doing everything we can to support those affected," officials said, adding that it was too soon to determine whether those killed were on the plane or in vehicles struck by the aircraft.

According to the authorities, the crash sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky and trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit, as well as some people in cars.

Investigation launched into cause of crash

The Prime Air aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire.

The NTSB said in an X post on Sunday the B-767-300 cargo airplane was flying into Miami from San Juan, Puerto Rico and they have "launched a go team to investigate Sunday's runway excursion accident."

The flight was operated by 21 Air, a North Carolina-based cargo carrier. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to Flightradar24.

Amazon said it would cooperate with the investigation.

“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport,” the company said in a statement. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones and all those affected by this devastating loss."

About 250 flights were delayed at the airport by late Sunday afternoon, according to FlightAware. Fire crews were still dealing with a fuel leak several hours later, according to reports.

Eyewitness say they saw 'thick black smoke billowing into the sky'

Jackson Lee, who runs an electronics shop near the crash site, told news agencies that he went outside with four colleagues after the crash and saw smoke rising near the airport’s fences.

"We hear planes taking off and landing every five minutes. I thought I’d got used to it," Lee said. "I never thought it could come this close to us."

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko
